rows.reference: Dhammapada 129 to 130 (Daṇḍavagga, chapter 10)
rows.original: sabbe tasanti daṇḍassa, sabbe bhāyanti maccuno; attānaṃ upamaṃ katvā, na haneyya na ghātaye
rows.says: All tremble at the rod and all fear death; life is dear to all. Putting yourself in the place of another, do not kill or strike, and do not make others do so.
rows.bearing: K1: Taught by a wider rule (rule 7). It forbids killing any being, and causing others to kill, with no exception, so it includes K1 and asks more (no defence exception). 'Sabbe' (all) reaches every person K1 protects, of any faith, status, sex or age, newborns included (rule 9). 'Do not cause to kill' reaches masters, parents and leaders who order a killing. K0: taught a fortiori. K3: the verse makes no exception for war (wider rule; war is context only, rule 5).

rows.reference: Saṃyutta Nikāya 55.7 (Veḷudvāreyya Sutta, 'The People of Bamboo Gate')
rows.original: pāṇātipātā paṭivirato (Pali phrase from memory, not seen in a search result)
rows.says: Taught to brahmin householders. A disciple reflects: I want to live and do not want to die; being killed would be unwelcome to me, and it is just as unwelcome to another, so how could I do it to them? He gives up killing, encourages others to give it up and praises doing so. The same reasoning is applied to theft, adultery and harmful speech.
rows.bearing: K1: Taught by a wider rule (rule 7), addressed to lay householders, so it binds private persons and heads of households; 'another' is unrestricted. K0: taught a fortiori.

rows.says: The canon treats killing one's mother, father or an arahant as among the gravest deeds. The commentaries say a killing needs a living being, knowledge that it is one, the intention to kill, an act, and death as a result, and they rate a killing as heavier or lighter by the victim's virtue and size and by the effort made.

rows.says: In a past life the Buddha, as a ship's captain, kills a man who is about to murder 500 merchants, out of compassion for the merchants and for the would-be murderer, and accepts the karmic cost himself. Asaṅga says a bodhisattva who, with a compassionate and troubled mind and no other way, kills a robber about to commit many murders incurs no fault and gains much merit.
rows.bearing: Within K1's own exception (a killing needed to stop someone from killing), and the motive is compassion, not gain, anger or revenge, so it does not contradict K1 or K0. It loosens the stricter Pali teaching (MN 21) for Mahāyāna only. Unverified, so it does not decide (rule 1).

rows.says: Reported: killing an icchantika (one said to have cut off all roots of goodness) is not among the three grades of killing and carries no karmic result of killing; and the Buddha, in a past life as King Sen'yo, killed brahmins who slandered the Mahāyāna sūtras and did not fall into hell for it. The Sen'yo story concerns a king (rule 5, context), though whether his act was judicial is disputed (rule 6). Bearing arms to defend monks would fall within K1's exception. Unverified, so it does not decide now (rule 1). This is the main open item for Buddhism.

support.reconciliation:
Theravāda. Its authorities are the Pali canon itself (Tier 1), Buddhaghosa's commentaries (Tier 2) and, for modern readings only, scholar-monks with no binding standing. The canon states the rule against killing with no exception: for lay people (SN 55.7 and Dhp 129 to 130, verified; Snp 2.14, MN 41 and AN 8.39, unverified) and for monks and nuns (Vinaya, Pārājika 3, unverified). It asks more than K1: it gives no exception for defence, and it forbids even hatred towards attackers (MN 21, verified). The monastic code lets a monk strike to get free when attacked (Pācittiya 74, verified in the households research), but nothing found extends this to killing. The commentaries define killing by five factors and grade its weight by the victim's virtue and size and by the effort made, and the canon counts killing a mother, father or arahant among the gravest deeds. This grades the wrong but permits no killing (graded protection, unverified). Theravāda places its chronicles below the canon. The Mahāvaṃsa's claim that the enemies killed in Duṭṭhagāmaṇī's war hardly counted as human is outside the corpus, and Dhp 129 to 130 ('sabbe', all) and SN 42.3 contradict it. Earlier project research found the Theravāda scholar-monk Ven. Dhammavihari Thera arguing that no killing, for any purpose, can be justified by the Buddha's teaching (a modern authority, binding no one; not re-checked here). The Milindapañha (Tier 2) treats a king's punishments as the wrongdoer's own deeds coming back to him; that concerns courts, so it is context only (unverified).

Mahāyāna. Its authorities are the Mahāyāna sūtras, which that branch treats as primary scripture, and the treatises of Asaṅga, Śāntideva and Nāgārjuna, which are authoritative but not primary. East Asian Mahāyāna takes the Brahmajāla bodhisattva precepts as its rule for lay people and clergy alike. The first major precept forbids killing any living being, and forbids causing, praising or rejoicing in a killing (unverified). Tibetan Mahāyāna follows the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya, whose third pārājika is reported to match the Pali (unverified), and Śāntideva's charge to protect all beings as oneself (Bodhicaryāvatāra 8.90, verified). Asaṅga's Bodhisattvabhūmi (ethics chapter) reads the skilful-means killing of the Upāyakauśalya Sūtra narrowly. It is allowed only to a bodhisattva who kills someone about to murder many, from compassion for both sides, with no other way, and accepting the karmic cost. That lies within K1's own exception (known only through scholarly reports). East Asian commentators are reported to read the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra's passages on icchantikas and King Sen'yo as hyperbole that stresses how grave it is to slander the Dharma. They set them against the same sūtra's later teaching that all beings, icchantikas included, have buddha-nature, and no school is reported to treat them as a rule of conduct. None of this is verified, and no classical commentator has yet been named or checked; a modern study to read is Ming-Wood Liu, 'The Problem of the Icchantika in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra' (JIABS, 1984). Theravāda does not accept these sūtras.

K1.label: Taught (wider rule)
K1.reason: Three verified Tier 1 Pali texts, Dhp 129 to 130, SN 55.7 and SN 3.8 = Ud 5.1, explicitly forbid killing or harming anyone. They make no exception, and their scope is unrestricted ('all', 'another'). SN 55.7 and SN 3.8 are taught to lay people, so these texts bind private persons and heads of households, and they protect everyone K1 protects, newborns included (rules 7 and 9). The Pali canon asks more than K1 (no defence exception, MN 21), and that still includes K1. No verified counted text was found that lets a private person kill outside K1's exception, and the Mahāyāna skilful-means killing falls within that exception. Caveats: (1) the Pali rows are counted for all branches on the Article I convention, but the Chinese and Tibetan parallels have not been checked; (2) the Mahāyāna branch's own primary rule (Brahmajāla major precept 1) is unverified, so for Mahāyāna the label rests on the shared early discourses and on Śāntideva (Tier 2); (3) the Mahāparinirvāṇa icchantika passage is unverified. If it is verified, East Asian Mahāyāna would become 'Unclear' (rule 6) or 'Contradicted in one branch' (rule 3), depending on whether the tradition's own texts and commentators narrow it.

K0.label: Taught (wider rule)
K0.reason: The same verified texts forbid all killing, so they forbid killing for gain, anger, hatred or revenge a fortiori. MN 21 (Tier 1, verified, Clear teaching) also forbids even inner hatred towards one's torturers. By their own terms the Mahāyāna skilful-means killings are done from compassion, not gain or anger. The Mahāparinirvāṇa caveat applies to K0 as it does to K1, since that passage would declare a killing blameless whatever the motive.

K3.label: Taught (wider rule); context only
K3.reason: Dhp 129 to 130 makes no exception for war. SN 42.3 (Tier 1, verified, Clear teaching) condemns a soldier's very intention to kill in battle, so killing those who are not fighting is condemned a fortiori. No counted text was found that names non-combatants as such or permits killing them. DN 26 (an ideal king who conquers without weapons) and SN 3.14 to 15 point the same way but are unverified. The main contrary text is the Mahāvaṃsa (chapter 25), which is outside the corpus and does not decide (rule 1).

Whoever kills an icchantika (one held to have cut off every root of goodness) falls into none of the three: like digging the earth, cutting grass or felling a tree, it carries no retribution. The brahmins King Sen'yo killed are said to have been icchantikas.

But the sutra's own later chapters, the Brahmajāla precepts and classical commentators narrow it (see the reconciliation rows), which points to Unclear (rule 6). The grading of the other killings by the victim's standing is graded protection, not permission (rule 2). Unverified, so it does not decide (rule 1).

counter.reconciliation: 1. Counted texts common to all branches. The first precept forbids killing any living being, and the early discourses state it without exception for status, faith, sex, age or household: Dhammapada 129 to 130 ('all tremble at the rod... do not kill or cause to kill'; Tier 1, VERIFIED (search)) and Saṃyutta Nikāya 55.7 (taught to lay people; Tier 1, VERIFIED (search)); Sutta Nipāta 394 adds a ban on approving another's killing (Tier 1, UNVERIFIED). For monastics the third pārājika rule (Tier 1, with parallels in the Dharmaguptaka and Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinayas used by the East Asian and Tibetan branches; UNVERIFIED in this run) expels anyone who kills a human, provides a weapon or urges death, with the same penalty whatever the victim's standing and, as recalled, no self-defence exception, though striking in self-defence is not an offence (Pācittiya 74, VERIFIED (search)). The early texts grade the weight of killing upward for parents and arahants (AN 5.129, UNVERIFIED) and Buddhaghosa's commentaries (Tier 2, Theravāda) grade it by the victim's virtue, but no counted or commentarial Theravāda text found declares any human killing blameless; that is graded protection, not permission. 2. Theravāda hard texts lie outside the canon. The Mahāvaṃsa's consolation of Duṭṭhagāmaṇī (chapter 25; outside the corpus; war) is subordinate in Theravāda's own ranking of texts, by which a claimed teaching is tested against the discourses and the monastic code (DN 16, the four great references; Tier 1, UNVERIFIED), and the canon contradicts it directly: Dhammapada 129 to 130, SN 42.3 (a soldier who dies set on killing goes to hell or animal birth; VERIFIED (search)) and MN 21 (no hatred even towards bandits sawing one apart; VERIFIED (search)). Ven. Dhammavihari Thera, a modern Theravāda scholar-monk (individual standing only), rejects the passage as contrary to the teaching (found in the Article I research, not re-checked). On courts, the Milindapañha (Tier 2, para-canonical) reconciles non-harm with royal punishment by saying the criminal's own deeds, not the teaching, bring his punishment, and DN 26, DN 5 and Jātaka 538 present executions as a sign of decline or a path to hell (all UNVERIFIED in this run). 3. Mahāyāna. The 'skill in means' killings (Upāyakauśalya Sūtra, a sutra treated as primary; Asaṅga's Bodhisattvabhūmi, a treatise authoritative especially for Tibetan bodhisattva vows) are confined by the texts themselves to killing someone about to commit mass murder, from compassion for both victims and killer, with no other means and with the killer accepting the karmic cost: this falls within K1's exception. Tsongkhapa's commentary on Asaṅga (Gelug authority) keeps these conditions (not checked). The Brahmajāla precepts (treated as primary in East Asian Mahāyāna only) forbid killing, praising or rejoicing at the killing of any being, and forbid revenge even for one's parents (UNVERIFIED in this run). Śāntideva (Bodhicaryāvatāra 8.90, treatise, VERIFIED (search)) asks the bodhisattva to protect all beings as himself. The hardest texts are the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra's story of King Sen'yo and its statement that killing an icchantika carries no retribution (treated as primary in Mahāyāna; UNVERIFIED). The tradition's own narrowings, none verified in this run, are: (a) the same sutra's later teaching that all beings, icchantikas included, have the Buddha-nature and can awaken, which removes the premise of the passage; (b) the sutra's framing of the king's act as compassion that brought the victims to faith and a Buddha-land, and its Diamond Body chapter, which lets lay people bear arms to protect monks but, as recalled, not to take life; (c) Nichiren (13th century; authority for the Nichiren schools only), who held that after Śākyamuni the instruction is to withhold alms from slanderers, not to kill them; (d) the Brahmajāla first precept for East Asian schools. Modern scholarship (for example Ming-Wood Liu, JIABS 1984, on the icchantika; outside the tradition) traces the passages to different layers of the text. No Mahāyāna school is known to treat the passage as a rule of conduct, but this was not verified. 4. Standing. Buddhism has no body with authority to interpret the texts for the whole tradition (corpus.md lists none), so reconciliations are by counted texts, classical commentators and school founders, each binding only its own branch or school. Vajrayāna 'liberation' rites and the Langdarma story are outside the corpus; Tibetan commentators read the tantric verses on killing as metaphors (not checked).

K1.label: Taught (Mahāyāna provisional: the Mahāparinirvāṇa passages are unverified)
K1.reason: Dhammapada 129 to 130 and SN 55.7 (Tier 1, Explicit, VERIFIED (search)) forbid killing anyone, by a wider rule that reaches every person (rule 7); they are Pali texts, and the Chinese and Tibetan parallels for the other branches were not checked, the same gap Article I recorded. No verified counted text permits a private killing outside K1's exception, approves killing newborns or children, or limits protection to one community. The Upāyakauśalya and Bodhisattvabhūmi killings stop a planned mass murder and fit the exception. The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra's Sen'yo story and icchantika passage (counted for Mahāyāna only) bear directly on K1 but are UNVERIFIED, so they do not decide (rule 1). If they are confirmed, the Mahāyāna result should be Unclear (rule 6), because the same sutra's Buddha-nature teaching, the Brahmajāla precepts and Nichiren narrow them and the paradigm killer is a king (rule 5 dispute); a reader who rejects those narrowings would label it Contradicted in one branch (Mahāyāna) under rules 2 and 3, since the icchantika passage declares a class of killings blameless because of who the victims are. The canonical and commentarial grading (AN 5.129; Buddhaghosa) is graded protection, not permission (rule 2).

K0.label: Taught
K0.reason: Dhammapada 129 to 130 (Explicit, wider rule) and MN 21 (Clear teaching: not even hatred towards bandits who are sawing one apart) are Tier 1 and VERIFIED (search), and teach K0 a fortiori. The Brahmajāla ban on revenge even for one's parents would add an Explicit East Asian Mahāyāna text but is unverified. The Mahāyāna killings in the hard texts are presented as acts of compassion, not of gain, anger or revenge; only a literal reading of the unverified icchantika passage, which ignores motive, would bear on K0, and it does not decide (rule 1).

K3.label: Taught (by a wider rule)
K3.reason: SN 42.3 (Tier 1, VERIFIED (search)) teaches at the level of Clear teaching that a soldier who dies set on killing 'these beings' goes to hell or animal birth, so it condemns killing anyone in battle, non-combatants included (rule 7); Dhammapada 129 to 130 is a further wider rule. Against it, the Mahāvaṃsa's consolation of Duṭṭhagāmaṇī is outside the corpus (rule 1), and the Satyakaparivarta (Mahāyāna, unverified) reportedly accepts defensive war but tells the king to capture enemies alive, which supports rather than contradicts K3. War remains context only for the floor.

A human being is counted from the mind's first appearance in the mother's womb until death. No offence only if it is unintended, unknown, not aimed at death, done while insane, or by the first offender; there is no self-defence clause.
rows.bearing: K1: Explicit for monks and nuns (who include teachers and religious leaders), with the same penalty whatever the victim's faith, status, sex or age; newborns are plainly inside the rule (rule 9; the part before birth is context). Stricter than K1 (no defence exception). Binds monastics only; lay duty rests on rows 1 to 8.

rows.original: 若自殺、教人殺、方便讚歎殺、見作隨喜乃至呪殺 ... 乃至一切有命者不得故殺

rows.branch: Theravāda (Pali Vinaya)
rows.reference: Vinaya, Pārājika 3: origin story pli-tv-bu-vb-pj3:1.1.13 to 1.1.29; cases 5.2 to 5.3 (accidents), 5.17 to 5.19 (abortion), 5.32 (executioner), 5.33 (relatives and a maimed man)

rows.says: Origin: a hired sham ascetic kills monks; a deity of Māra's realm praises him for 'making merit', and the Buddha then lays down the rule. Cases: crushing a hidden boy by accident is no offence (unintended); causing an abortion that kills the child is expulsion; a monk who tells an executioner to kill a prisoner with one blow is expelled; a monk or nun who, when a maimed man's relatives say they want him dead, suggests a drink that kills him is expelled.
rows.bearing: Rule 4: the only approval of killing comes from Māra's side and is condemned. Before birth and accident are context (exclusions c, f). The executioner case is court context (rule 5) but shows a monk may not even urge an execution. The relatives' case shows the rule protects a household member against his family's wish (supports K1 for monastic agents; it also touches exclusion d).

rows.branch: Mahāyāna: East Asian (Dharmakṣema's Chinese read; also in the Southern recension T375, juan 11, p. 676a24); standing in the Tibetan Kangyur not checked; not accepted by Theravāda
rows.reference: Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, chapter 7 'Holy Practice' (聖行品), Taishō T12 no. 374, juan 12, p. 434c08 to c21
rows.original: 我念往昔，於此閻浮提作大國王，名曰仙預 ... 聞婆羅門誹謗方等，聞已即時斷其命根
rows.translation: Verifier's own rendering from the Chinese
rows.says: The Buddha says that in a past life he was a great king, Sen'yo, who served brahmins for twelve years; when he heard them slander the Mahāyāna scriptures he at once took their lives, and because of this he has not since fallen into hell. Protecting the Mahāyāna has such power.
rows.bearing: The founder within the text approves a killing for speech against the teaching (rule 4 does not save it). The killer is a king, but there is no trial ('at once'), so whether it is judicial or private is disputed (rules 5 and 6). Read with rows 27 and 28.

rows.branch: Mahāyāna: East Asian (T374; T375 juan 15, p. 702b05); Tibetan standing not checked; not accepted by Theravāda
rows.reference: Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, chapter 8 'Brahma-conduct' (梵行品), T12 no. 374, juan 16, p. 459a20 to 460a14 (Kāśyapa's question and the answer on the Sen'yo killing)
rows.original: 菩薩摩訶薩乃至蟻子尚不故殺 ... 以愛念故，斷其命根，非惡心也 ... 若有眾生謗大乘者，即以鞭撻，苦加治之，或奪其命
rows.translation: Verifier's own rendering from the Chinese
rows.says: Kāśyapa asks how a bodhisattva who sees all beings as his only child could have killed the brahmins. The Buddha answers: a bodhisattva does not deliberately kill even an ant, and never takes beings' lives; he had reached that stage and cut off their lives out of love, not with an evil mind. As parents with an only son who breaks the state's law may, out of fear, banish or kill him without an evil mind, so a bodhisattva protecting the true teaching whips, harshly punishes, or takes the life of beings who slander the Mahāyāna, to make them reform. The brahmins, reborn in hell, understood why, gained faith and were reborn in a Buddha's land with a life of ten aeons: 'how can that be called killing?'
rows.bearing: Missed by both researchers and wider than the Sen'yo story: it states as a general matter, not only for kings, that a bodhisattva protecting the teaching may take the life of those who slander the Mahāyāna (victims marked out by belief and speech). This bears directly on K1 (heretics and unbelievers are inside K1's protection). The same passage narrows it: the agent is a bodhisattva at the 'only-child' stage acting from love, not an evil mind, and the sūtra says a bodhisattva never deliberately kills. The parents image is an image only (rule 4, Implied). Motive is stated to be love, not gain, anger, hatred or revenge, so it does not cut against K0. Supports Unclear for Mahāyāna (rule 6); a reader who gives the general statement full weight would say Contradicted in one branch (rule 3).

rows.branch: Mahāyāna: East Asian (T374; T375 juan 15, p. 702c20); Tibetan standing not checked; not accepted by Theravāda
rows.reference: Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, chapter 8 'Brahma-conduct' (梵行品), T12 no. 374, juan 16, p. 460a15 to b21 (three grades of killing; the icchantika)
rows.original: 若有能殺一闡提者，則不墮此三種殺中 ... 殺一闡提亦復如是，無有罪報
rows.translation: Verifier's own rendering from the Chinese
rows.says: Kāśyapa says, and the Buddha agrees, that beings fall into hell because of an evil mind. The Buddha then sets out three grades of killing: lower (animals), middle (ordinary people up to non-returners), upper (parents, arhats, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas of the fixed stage), each with its hell. Whoever kills an icchantika falls into none of the three; like digging earth or cutting grass, killing an icchantika carries no retribution. The brahmins (of the Sen'yo story) were all icchantikas, lacking faith and the other four roots.
rows.bearing: The hardest Buddhist text for K1: a counted text for Mahāyāna declares the killing of a class of people blameless because of who they are (rule 2 wording, one branch: rule 3). For K0 the sūtra's own condition (no hell where there is no evil mind, 460a17 to a26) and Huiyuan's gloss (row 30) tie it to killing without evil intent. The grading of other killings is graded protection (rule 2). Narrowed by the same sūtra (rows 13, 29, 31) and by the Brahmajāla (row 14) for East Asia, but affirmed by the classical commentators checked (row 30): Unclear (rule 6), close to Contradicted in one branch.

rows.branch: Mahāyāna: East Asian (T374; T375 juan 3, p. 624b01 to b02); not accepted by Theravāda
rows.reference: Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, chapter 2 'Diamond Body' (金剛身品), T12 no. 374, juan 3, p. 383c27 to 384b11
rows.original: 為護法故，雖持刀杖，我說是等名為持戒。雖持刀杖，不應斷命
rows.translation: Verifier's own rendering from the Chinese
rows.says: King Possessing Virtue fights precept-breaking monks who attack the teacher Realised Virtue with weapons, is wounded all over, dies and is reborn in Akṣobhya's land. Lay protectors of the teaching should carry weapons to guard monks who keep the precepts; the text even says that those who, to protect the teaching, do not take the five precepts are the true Mahāyāna people. But kings, ministers and lay followers who carry weapons to protect the teaching 'should not take life'; doing so is the highest keeping of the precepts.
rows.bearing: Armed defence of a teacher under attack fits K1's exception. The closing line is the sūtra's own limit on its lay protectors (rule 6 narrowing of rows 26 to 28 for ordinary followers). It also sets aside the five precepts for armed protectors, which shows the tension inside the text.

rows.tier: outside the corpus (classical East Asian commentators; reported as the tradition's own reading, METHOD.md section 9, decision 7)
rows.branch: East Asian Mahāyāna (Huiyuan: Dilun and general Sui exegesis; Guanding: Tiantai school)
rows.reference: Huiyuan of Jingying Temple, Da banniepan jing yiji (T37 no. 1764), juan 5, p. 755b10 to b17 and 756a17 to b05; Guanding, Da banniepan jing shu (T38 no. 1767), juan 8, p. 84c14 to c24; juan 17, p. 141b16 to b21; juan 28, p. 198b27 to b29
rows.original: 以知闡提全無善根，殺無惡意，是故無罪 (Huiyuan); 若據闡提現在無善，害之無罪 (Guanding); 昔時平而法弘，應持戒勿持仗；今時險而法翳，應持仗勿持戒 (Guanding)
rows.translation: Verifier's own rendering from the Chinese
rows.says: Huiyuan: the brahmins wholly lacked roots of goodness; one who kills knowing this, without evil intent, incurs no fault. Guanding: since an icchantika now has no goodness, harming him is no fault; an icchantika carries grave evil, so killing him is no fault while killing a mosquito is. On the Diamond Body chapter, Guanding says that when times are peaceful one should keep the precepts and not carry arms, and when times are perilous one should carry arms rather than keep the precepts.
rows.bearing: These are the earliest classical commentators found, and they do not read the passages as hyperbole: they explain and affirm that killing an icchantika is without fault. Huiyuan narrows it to one who knows the victim's roots and kills without evil intent (agent and motive), which bears on K0 but not on K1. So the narrowing for K1 rests on the sūtra itself and the Brahmajāla, not on these commentators. Outside the corpus; cannot decide a label (rule 1).

rows.check: added by verifier; it corrects both researchers' unverified statement that East Asian commentators read the passage as hyperbole

rows.branch: Mahāyāna: East Asian (T374)
rows.reference: Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, T12 no. 374: juan 22 (ch. 10), p. 493b19 to b21 and 493c24 to c26; juan 27 (ch. 11, Lion's Roar), p. 524c01 to c04; juan 35 (ch. 12, Kāśyapa), p. 570c18 to c20 and 571c19 to c20; contrary statements juan 26, p. 519a10 to a12 and 519b04 to b05
rows.original: 我常宣說一切眾生悉有佛性，乃至一闡提等亦有佛性 ... 一闡提等定當得成阿耨多羅三藐三菩提
rows.translation: Verifier's own rendering from the Chinese

But juan 26 also says icchantikas truly cannot attain awakening and lack Buddha-nature.
rows.bearing: Removes, in part, the premise of row 28 (that such people are beyond all goodness), so it is the sūtra's own narrowing (rule 6). Guanding (row 30) answers it by saying they lack goodness now, so the narrowing is itself disputed. Supports Unclear, not Taught.

missed_counter_evidence: Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra T374 juan 16, p. 459c26 to 460a05 (both researchers missed it). As a general statement, not tied to a king, a bodhisattva who protects the true teaching 'whips, harshly punishes, or takes the life' of beings who slander the Mahāyāna, to make them reform. The text compares this to parents who, fearing the state's law, banish or kill an only son who broke it, 'without an evil mind'. This is wider than the Sen'yo story and bears on zealots and on protection limited by belief.

Classical commentators Huiyuan (T1764) and Guanding (T1767) affirm, rather than soften, the statement that killing an icchantika carries no fault. On the Diamond Body chapter, Guanding also says that in perilous times one should carry arms rather than keep the precepts (T1767 juan 8, p. 84c21 to c24).

Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra T374 juan 3, p. 384a24 to a26: those who keep the five precepts are 'not called Mahāyāna people', and those who, to protect the teaching, do not take the five precepts are. This suspends the lay precepts for armed protectors, although the same passage then says they 'should not take life' (p. 384b10).

Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra T374 juan 26, p. 519a10 to a12 and 519b04 to b05: icchantikas 'truly cannot attain awakening' and 'have no Buddha-nature'. This cuts against the reconciliation that relies on the later chapters' teaching that icchantikas have Buddha-nature (juan 22, 27, 35).

Satyakaparivarta T272 juan 5, p. 338a14 to a17: defensive war fought with three compassionate intentions is 'meritorious and without fault', and any killing in it is a slight fault removable by repentance (war context only).

Searched for and not found in the texts read: any counted text permitting the killing of newborns, children, slaves or servants, or of wives by husbands; any Pali canonical text approving a deliberate killing of a person; any text allowing blood revenge (the Brahmajāla forbids it even for one's parents or ruler). Pārājika 3, case 5.33 (relatives who want a maimed man dead) shows the monastic rule protecting a household member against his family's wish.
verified.reconciliation:
Theravāda. Its counted texts are the Pali canon. The Theravāda commentaries and the Milindapañha are authoritative (Tier 2) but not primary. The canon, read here directly in SuttaCentral's source text, forbids killing anyone. It makes no exception for faith, status, sex, age or household. For lay people this is in Dhp 129 to 130, SN 55.7, SN 3.8 (= Ud 5.1), MN 41, AN 8.39 and Snp 394, and Snp 394 also forbids having others kill or permitting killing. For monks and nuns it is Pārājika 3. Its word-analysis counts a human being from the first mind in the womb, so infants are plainly covered, and its non-offence list has no self-defence clause. Its cases make it expulsion to urge an executioner on, or to help relatives who want a maimed family member dead. The canon asks more than K1. MN 21 forbids even a hostile thought towards bandits who are sawing one apart. Pācittiya 74 lets a monk strike only to free himself. Killing a parent or an arahant is graded heavier (AN 5.129; the Mahāvagga bars on ordination), which is graded protection, not permission. No Pali canonical passage was found that approves a deliberate killing of a person. MN 86 and the origin story of Pārājika 3 report killings and condemn them, and the only voice that praises killing comes from Māra's realm. DN 26, DN 5 and the Ratnāvalī treat royal executions as a sign of decline or as something to avoid (context). Theravāda's own rule for ranking texts (DN 16, the four great references) places the Mahāvaṃsa below the canon, and the canon contradicts its consolation of Duṭṭhagāmaṇī (Dhp 129 to 130; SN 42.3). Buddhaghosa's grading of the weight of killing and the Milindapañha's reconciliation of royal punishment remain unverified.

Mahāyāna. Its counted texts are the Mahāyāna sūtras, treated as primary, and the early-text parallels in its own canons. The rule against killing is verified there. East Asia has the Chinese Dharmapada verse matching Dhp 129 (T210), Saṃyukta Āgama 1044 matching SN 55.7, the Dharmaguptaka Vinaya's third pārājika, and the Brahmajāla bodhisattva precepts for lay and ordained. The Brahmajāla's first major precept forbids killing, or causing, praising or rejoicing in the killing of, any living being. Its light precepts forbid keeping weapons, joining armies, and taking revenge even for one's parents or ruler. For Tibet, the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya's third pārājika was read in Yijing's Chinese and expressly protects the human embryo; the Tibetan text was not read. The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra itself quotes the Dhammapada verse (juan 10).

The hard texts are in the same sūtra (Dharmakṣema's version, verified). (a) As King Sen'yo, the Buddha took the lives of brahmins as soon as he heard them slander the Mahāyāna (juan 12). (b) Explaining this, the sūtra says that a bodhisattva protecting the teaching may whip, punish or take the life of those who slander the Mahāyāna (juan 16). (c) It also says that whoever kills an icchantika incurs no retribution, as with cutting grass (juan 16). The sūtra narrows these in its own text in four ways. A bodhisattva 'does not deliberately kill even an ant' and never takes life, and the Sen'yo act was done by one at the stage of loving all beings as an only child, from love and not an evil mind, and the victims were reborn in a Buddha's land ('how can that be called killing?'). Hell follows an evil mind (juan 16). Lay followers who carry weapons to protect the teaching 'should not take life' (juan 3). Icchantikas have Buddha-nature and will awaken (juan 22, 27, 35), although juan 26 says the opposite.

The classical commentators checked do not soften the icchantika passage. Huiyuan (Sui) holds it blameless where the killer knows the victim's state and has no evil intent. Guanding (Tiantai) holds it blameless because the icchantika now lacks all goodness. Guanding also allows bearing arms in perilous times. Nichiren reportedly limited the passages, after Śākyamuni's time, to withholding alms from slanderers (outside the corpus, for Nichiren schools only, unverified).

The skilful-means killings are confined to stopping someone about to murder many, after other means fail, from compassion, with the killer accepting hell. This is the Upāyakauśalya's caravan leader (T346) and the Bodhisattvabhūmi's robber (T1579). It falls within K1's own exception. The Bodhisattvabhūmi handles a cruel official by removal from office, not killing. The Satyakaparivarta and the Ratnāvalī tell kings not to execute or maim, and in war to capture alive where possible (context).

Standing. Buddhism has no body with authority to interpret the texts for the whole tradition (corpus.md names none). Reconciliations rest on counted texts, classical commentators and school founders, each binding only its own branch or school.

K1.label: Unclear (Mahāyāna branch); Taught by a wider rule in Theravāda
K1.reason: Theravāda: Taught (rule 7). Verified Tier 1 Pali texts (Dhp 129 to 130, SN 55.7, SN 3.8, Snp 394, MN 41, AN 8.39) forbid killing anyone and having anyone killed, for lay people, with unrestricted scope, newborns included (rule 9). Pārājika 3 does the same for monastics. No counted Pali text permits a private killing. Mahāyāna: the wider rule is also verified in counted texts: the Chinese Dharmapada, SA 1044, the Dharmaguptaka and Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinayas, the Brahmajāla first major precept (East Asia), and the Mahāparinirvāṇa's own quotation of the verse. But the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, which Mahāyāna treats as primary, says three things in verified passages (T374 juan 12 and 16). Killing an icchantika carries no retribution because of who the victim is. A bodhisattva protecting the teaching may take the lives of those who slander the Mahāyāna. The Buddha as King Sen'yo did so at once on hearing them. Taken alone, these fit rule 3 (Contradicted in one branch), and the classical commentators checked (Huiyuan, Guanding) affirm the no-fault reading. The label is Unclear (rule 6) rather than Contradicted because the same counted sūtra narrows its reach in four ways. It says a bodhisattva never deliberately kills, not even an ant. It confines the act to a bodhisattva at the 'only-child' stage acting from love. It tells armed lay protectors that they 'should not take life'. Its later chapters teach that icchantikas will awaken. For East Asia, the Brahmajāla also forbids killing any being. The paradigm killer is also a king acting without trial, so whether the act is judicial or private is disputed (rules 5 and 6). This depends on a disputed reading. A reader who gives the 'no retribution' sentence and the commentators full weight would label it Contradicted in one branch (Mahāyāna). The Tibetan branch's acceptance of these passages was not checked. The Upāyakauśalya and Bodhisattvabhūmi killings fall within K1's exception and do not affect the label.

K0.label: Taught (wider rule; Explicit against revenge in East Asian Mahāyāna)
K0.reason: Theravāda: Dhp 129 to 130 (Explicit, wider rule), SN 55.7 and MN 21 (Clear teaching: no hostility even towards torturers), with Dhp 3 to 5 against hatred and grudges; all verified directly. East Asian Mahāyāna: the Brahmajāla first major precept forbids killing any being, and killing 'with an indulgent, pleased mind' is a defeat. Its tenth and twenty-first light precepts forbid revenge even when one's parents, kin or ruler are killed (Explicit). The hard Mahāparinirvāṇa killings are said to be done from love, 'not with an evil mind'. The same passage says that hell follows an evil mind, and Huiyuan reads the icchantika statement as covering only killing without evil intent. So no counted text licenses killing for gain, anger, hatred or revenge. Caveat: Guanding's gloss on the icchantika passage names no condition of motive. A face-value reading of T374 p. 460b15 to 21 alone would make Mahāyāna Unclear for K0 too, but the sūtra's own surrounding text resolves it against such a reading.

K3.label: Taught (wider rule); context only
K3.reason: SN 42.3 (Tier 1, Clear teaching, verified directly) condemns the very intention to kill in battle, so killing those who are not fighting is condemned a fortiori (rule 7). Dhp 129 to 130 has no war exception. For East Asian Mahāyāna, the Brahmajāla's eleventh light precept keeps bodhisattvas out of armies, and its first major precept forbids all killing. The Satyakaparivarta (Mahāyāna, verified in Chinese) accepts defensive war but tells the king to subdue without battle where possible and to capture alive rather than kill. SN 3.15 shows a captured enemy king released alive, and DN 26 an ideal ruler who conquers 'without rod or sword' (context). No counted text names non-combatants as a class or permits killing them. The Mahāvaṃsa's dismissal of slain unbelievers is outside the corpus (rule 1). War remains context for the floor (rule 5).

verified.fairness_notes:
1. The Mahāyāna label is a judgement on a disputed reading. Under the brief's rule 2, a text that declares a killing blameless 'because of who the victim is' counts as contradicting. T374 p. 460b15 to 21 says exactly that of icchantikas, and the classical commentators checked agree. The verifier chose Unclear because the same sūtra limits who may act and forbids armed protectors to kill. An adherent of another tradition whose hard text was ruled Contradicted, despite a general ban on killing elsewhere in its scripture, could fairly ask whether the same narrowing would have been allowed for them. The project lead should compare this with how the Hebrew Bible's zealot and enticer texts and comparable passages are labelled, and apply one standard.

2. In the other direction, a Mahāyāna adherent could object that Buddhism is being judged by a few sentences of one sūtra that no school is known to use as a rule of conduct. East Asian practice is governed by the Brahmajāla precepts, which forbid all killing and all revenge. The report says this, but the label still turns on the sūtra, as rule 1 requires for any text a branch treats as primary.

3. Asymmetric scrutiny. Buddhism's hard texts were confirmed only because the Pali and Chinese canons happen to be readable as source files from this environment. Other traditions whose hard texts remain UNVERIFIED (because searches failed) may look better by comparison. Buddhism should not appear worse merely because its texts were easier to check.

4. Rows 1 to 12 now rest on direct reading of source text, while most other traditions rest on search results. This is a stronger check, not a different standard of what counts.

5. The Pali Vinaya's lack of a self-defence exception asks more than K1. It was not treated as a contradiction, consistent with K1 being a floor.

6. The Mahāvaṃsa is a chronicle and was kept outside the corpus, as chronicles are for other traditions. It is reported beside the label and not used against Theravāda.

7. Using the Chinese Dharmapada (T210) as a counted Tier 1 parallel extends corpus.md's wording, which names the Āgamas and two Vinayas. This is flagged for the project lead so that it is not read as a favour to East Asian Buddhism.

8. The word 'icchantika' (one held to have cut off the roots of goodness) is a technical term whose reach is itself disputed within the sūtra (juan 26 against juan 27). The report records both sides rather than choosing one.
